name: Positional Hierarchy
description: A priority map for knowing when to survive, escape, sweep, pass, pin, or finish. The positional hierarchy is the decision-making framework that separates chaotic grappling from systematic BJJ.
shortInstruction: Ranking from worst to best: back taken → mounted → side control → knee on belly → guard bottom → half guard top → side control top → mount → back taken (you on top). Always know where you are on the hierarchy and what your objective is.
summary: The positional hierarchy ranks grappling positions from most vulnerable to most dominant. The system dictates your tactical objective at every position: if you are in a bottom position (worse), your goal is to escape. If you are in a top position (better), your goal is to advance or submit. Every decision you make should be filtered through this hierarchy — do not attempt a submission from a position where you do not have positional dominance first.
whyItWorks: The hierarchy gives you a clear objective at every moment — there is no confusion about what to do next
Attempting submissions from inferior positions against skilled opponents fails at a high rate — the hierarchy tells you when submissions are viable and when to prioritize escape
Understanding the hierarchy prevents you from wasting energy on low-percentage techniques from bad positions
The hierarchy is universal across all grappling sports (BJJ, wrestling, judo, MMA) — it is the shared language of positional control
commonMistakes: Attempting submissions from guard bottom when you should be sweeping or escaping first
Trying to pass guard when you are in half guard bottom — your objective at half guard bottom is to escape to neutral or guard, not to pass
Accepting a worse position because you are trying a low-percentage submission (e.g., giving up mount to try a kimura from bottom)
Not recognizing when the hierarchy shifts — a transition that moves you up one level is more valuable than a submission attempt that will likely fail
coachingCues: Know your position, know your goal
Do not chase submissions from bad positions
One level up is always a win
safetySummary: Do not sacrifice position for a low-percentage submission — positional reversals can cause injury when both grapplers are scrambling for control
Accepting a worse position (e.g., giving up side control) to attempt a submission is higher risk for injury than it is worth in training
When you are in a clearly inferior position, prioritize breathing and survival before attempting the escape — panic movements increase injury risk

systemLogic.corePrinciple: The positional hierarchy ranks grappling positions from most vulnerable (back taken) to most dominant (submission). Your tactical objective at every position is determined by your place on the hierarchy: below opponent = escape up, above opponent = advance forward.

decisionTree.condition: You are in bottom side control, mount, or back taken
decisionTree.action: Your objective is to ESCAPE up the hierarchy. Do not attempt submissions from these positions — focus on regaining guard or reversing position.

decisionTree.condition: You are in bottom guard or half guard
decisionTree.action: Your primary objective is to sweep or escape to a neutral/top position. Submissions are lower percentage from here — prioritize positional advancement first.

decisionTree.condition: You have top position (side control, mount, back)
decisionTree.action: Your objective is to ADVANCE to a more dominant position or submit. Stabilize the position before attacking — do not rush the submission attempt.

decisionTree.condition: You keep losing position while trying to submit
decisionTree.action: You are skipping levels on the hierarchy. Go back to securing positional dominance before attacking. One level up is always a win.

decisionTree.condition: You keep getting stuck at one hierarchy level
decisionTree.action: You are missing escape or transition techniques for that specific level. Drill 1-2 high-percentage transitions from your most common stuck position.

exitStrategies: Advancing one level (e.g., Side Control Bottom → Half Guard Bottom) is a tactical win even without scoring points — multiple small advances compound into scoring positions.
If the opponent operates outside the traditional hierarchy (leg lock specialist, guard puller), recognize they are playing a different game and adjust your strategy accordingly.
After advancing a level, spend 2-3 seconds stabilizing before moving to the next level to prevent reversals.

moneyDetails: The positional hierarchy is the single most important conceptual framework in BJJ — it tells you what to do at every moment of the match
Competition BJJ is won by advancing up the hierarchy faster and more consistently than the opponent
Understanding the hierarchy prevents the most common mistake in BJJ: attempting submissions before establishing positional control
The hierarchy is why Gracie jiu-jitsu emphasizes positional dominance before submissions — it has been tested for a century
fixItFast: If you are in a bad position and not sure what to do: check the hierarchy. You are in bottom side control — your goal is side control escape, not a submission
If you have top position and cannot submit: advance up the hierarchy. Side control → mount → back mount creates exponentially higher submission probability
If you keep getting reversed: you are skipping the 'secure position' step. After advancing a level, spend 2-3 seconds stabilizing before moving to the next level
